name: Morpheus8 (RF microneedling)

card.summary: InMode fractional radiofrequency microneedling device marketed for skin tightening and subdermal fat remodeling along the jawline and neck; evidence is mainly case series and reviews.
card.note: Grokipedia reports the FDA has noted risks such as burns, scarring and unintended fat loss with RF microneedling; a 2026 paper describes fibrosis and surgical complexity after nonsurgical treatments.

quick.overview:
Morpheus8 is a handheld device from InMode that combines microneedling with bipolar radiofrequency (RF) energy. Needles penetrate the skin to set depths and deliver heat to the dermis and subdermal layers, with the stated aims of stimulating collagen, tightening skin and remodeling a small amount of fat.

It is used on the face and neck, including the jawline and jowls, as a lower-downtime option for mild to moderate laxity. Reviews and retrospective series report improvements, but no randomized comparison against surgery was found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Insulated microneedles create channels in the skin while RF energy heats tissue at depths that Grokipedia says reach up to 8 mm. The resulting controlled injury is described as triggering a healing response with new collagen, and deeper settings are said to coagulate subdermal fat. It is often combined with FaceTite or liposuction.
quick.risks: Described risks include burns, scarring, pigmentation changes and unintended fat loss. A 2026 surgical paper reports that fibrosis and fat loss after nonsurgical treatments can complicate later neck lift surgery.

lead: Morpheus8 is a fractional radiofrequency microneedling device made by InMode that combines microneedles with bipolar RF energy to heat the dermis and subdermal tissue. Manufacturers and practitioners describe it as promoting collagen production, tightening skin and remodeling adipose tissue on the face, neck and body.[1][2]

It grew out of InMode's Fractora fractional RF platform; a 2020 study describes a combination of FaceTite bipolar RF and a fractional bipolar RF device (Fractora modified to Morpheus8) for lower face and neck laxity.[3] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports commercial introduction around 2018, US FDA clearance in 2020 for electrocoagulation and hemostasis, and a further clearance in 2024 for soft tissue contraction.[1]

Reviews in dermatology and facial plastic surgery present RF microneedling as a minimally invasive option for skin laxity, acne scarring and rejuvenation,[2][4] while the published evidence on jawline and fat remodeling consists largely of retrospective series and combination reports.[3][5][6]

paras: A 2022 review in Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology describes Morpheus8 as fractional RF microneedling that treats concerns from skin laxity to acne and scarring with reduced downtime compared with historically more invasive approaches.[2] A second 2022 review, in facial plastic surgery, states that RF microneedling is considered a safe and effective treatment for various aesthetic and dermatologic conditions in all skin types and highlights what differentiates Morpheus8 from other devices.[4]

Grokipedia reports several tip configurations, including resurfacing, intermediate and deep subdermal tips and a body tip, and says treatment depth is adjustable.[1] Because this source is AI-generated, device specifications should be checked against the manufacturer.

A 2020 retrospective review evaluated FaceTite bipolar RF combined with a fractional bipolar RF device modified to Morpheus8 for laxity of the lower face and neck.[3] A 2019 paper on adjustable-depth fractional RF with bipolar RF describes the combination as a treatment for patients between younger patients wanting tightening without surgery and those with laxity not severe enough for an excisional procedure.[7] A 2021 paper reported using RF-assisted lipolysis with RF microneedling for premature jowl and neck laxity after face-lift surgery.[5]
A 2025 paper describes combining low-energy Morpheus8 with nanofat grafting for compartment-specific facial rejuvenation, reporting selective fat remodeling and skin quality enhancement.[8]

Fractional RF has also been studied in acne and scarring and in hidradenitis suppurativa. A 2025 paper in Aesthetic Surgery Journal examined fractional RF for long-term acne remission and reduction of acne scar load,[9] and a 2026 retrospective study in Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology reported on fractional microneedling RF in hidradenitis suppurativa across anatomical sites.[10]

Grokipedia reports that the FDA has noted risks of RF microneedling devices including burns, scarring and unintended fat loss.[1] A 2026 paper in Aesthetic Surgery Journal describes fibrosis, fat loss and increased surgical complexity in patients who undergo neck lift after nonsurgical treatments.[11] A 2024 review discusses the role of noninvasive and minimally invasive techniques alongside open surgical procedures for body contouring.[12]

Human evidence is mainly retrospective reviews and case series. Examples include a 2020 retrospective review of combined RF in lower face and neck laxity,[3] a 2022 dermatology review,[2] a 2022 facial plastic surgery review,[4] a 2021 report on jowl and neck laxity after facelift,[5] and a 2025 paper combining Morpheus8 and nanofat grafting.[8] No randomized trial comparing Morpheus8 with surgery for jawline contour was found in the sources reviewed.
The procedure is categorized under hardmaxxing as a way to tighten and remodel tissue along the jawline and neck. Community discussion was not included in the sources reviewed.

timeline.event: US FDA clearance for electrocoagulation and hemostasis; US patent for the fractional RF technology (per Grokipedia).[1]
Further FDA clearance for soft tissue contraction (per Grokipedia).[1]
